hook: Complain in German the way it works: concede a little, then hold firm.
intro: A complaint that only complains gets a form letter back. One that concedes a point first and then presses is harder to brush off, and that concessive turn is what this exercise is for. Write 600 to 1300 characters. The strongest version is unemotional: dates, amounts and what you want, with the Konjunktiv II doing the politeness so the content can stay hard. Set a deadline, and say what you will do if it passes.
tips[0].title: Three ways to concede, one meaning
tips[0].text: obwohl takes a clause with the verb at the end. zwar … aber keeps two main clauses. trotz takes a noun in the genitive. Pick by what you have to hand: a clause, a pair of statements, or a noun.
tips[0].check.why: A noun phrase follows, so it takes the preposition trotz, not the conjunction obwohl.
tips[0].trap: trotz governs the genitive in writing: trotz mehrfacher Zusagen, not trotz mehrfachen Zusagen.
tips[1].title: Facts complain better than adjectives
tips[1].text: Unacceptable and terrible can be waved away; a date and an amount cannot. Give the order number, the dates, the sums, and what was promised against what happened. Let the reader draw the conclusion you have made unavoidable.
tips[1].check.why: A figure is checkable; a judgement is not.
tips[2].title: A deadline with a consequence
tips[2].text: A request with no date is a wish. Name a date, say what you expect by it, and say what follows if it passes. The Konjunktiv II keeps the tone civil while the content stays firm.
tips[2].check.why: Only a date can pass, which is what gives the request force.
tips[2].visual.moves[0].label: Concede
tips[2].visual.moves[1].label: Facts
tips[2].visual.moves[2].label: Demand
tips[2].visual.moves[3].label: Deadline
remember[0]: obwohl plus clause, zwar … aber plus two main clauses, trotz plus genitive noun.
remember[2]: Konjunktiv II for the tone, hard content underneath.
remember[3]: A deadline, and what happens after it.
exam: A written complaint is one of the B2 writing tasks, and in Germany it is the letter that actually gets things fixed.
mistakes[0].why: trotz takes the genitive in written German.
mistakes[1].why: obwohl sends the verb to the end of its clause.
mistakes[2].why: The fact is harder to dismiss than the judgement.
mistakes[3].why: A vague threat is weaker than a dated, specific one.
